9	## Dispatch and overloading
10	
11	**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance that the argument types allow, not at one only.
12	
13	**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
14	
15	**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
16	
17	**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object at each call, not at load (row 780).
18	
19	**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
20	
21	- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
22	- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
23	
24	The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method is an overload for this rule too. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or, where the trait itself extends `Number`, `excludes { HasRank }`, the trait that arrays extend. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.
25	
26	## Traits and objects
27	
28	**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
29	
30	**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. So where the Meet Rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads, several declarations that together cover the meet serve. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
31	
32	**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. The checker refuses such a redeclaration where an object reaches the method of a generic self-typed trait along two paths (row 1037; `compiler.md`, "The checker's gaps", gives the form). An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier, so a program that writes one does not compile (row 650).
33	
34	**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk and the checker stop the search for a cover at the same limits, which `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", gives. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).
35	
36	**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:
37	
38	- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
39	- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.
40	
41	In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` at `X` runs, also from an arm of a conditional or a `case` expression, a function expression or a local function. One shape fails the JVM's verification when its class loads: a `typecase` with `self` in one arm and another value in the other (row 1070). In that arm, bind `self` at the returned type, as `do r: X = self; r end`. A compiled body that `T` gives one of its methods can call a method on a value of type `X`. For a generic object that lists `T` first in its `extends` clause, no test covers such a body (row 1052). Before a compiled program relies on one, write a compiled test of it.
42	
43	When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. In two cases walk does not read `self` so, and its load check refuses the valid pair (row 999):
44	
45	- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
46	- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
47	
48	**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values take a subscript, as `a[i]`: an array, for example. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library.
49	
50	Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. A numeral at a parameter of type `Index` takes its default, a `ZZ32`, so `f(3)` is valid for `f(x: Index)`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Two departures:
51	
52	- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
53	- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).
54	
55	**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. Walk departs for numbers of two run-time types at one position: it refuses them, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Where the deciding elements' own comparison is `Unordered`, the answer is `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.
56	
57	**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:
58	
59	- values of different types are never equivalent;
60	- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
61	- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
62	- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.
63	
64	So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `true`. Two string literals joined by `||` fold into one ("Numbers"), so `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"` is `true`. A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ("Numbers"), so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `RR64` 0.5. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false` (row 923). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).

66	## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
67	
68	**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: in a generic object whose `T` stayed open, a call `pick((1, 2))` of its methods `pick(x: Any)` and `pick(x: (T,T))` runs the first (row 663). Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
69	
70	- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
71	- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
72	- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
73	
74	**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
75	
76	**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
77	
78	- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
79	- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
80	
81	The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension without its condition (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
82	
83	**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
84	
85	**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call runs only under walk, also after the switch-over. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, which lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.

87	## Numbers
88	
89	**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** In both libraries, seven are value objects (P-178): `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `RR32` and `RR64`. In the interpreter's library, `QQ` is a trait, and its values are the value object `Ratio` (P-166). The compiler's prelude declares no `QQ`. Do not extend a number type in a program. Declare a program's own number type below `Number` (P-160). Such a type runs on both paths. Both paths refuse an object declaration below one of the seven, as `object Mine extends ZZ32`. Walk refuses it at load: 'Attempt to extend object type ZZ32'. The compiled checker refuses it: 'Invalid type in extends clause: ZZ32'. The record calls this design route A, and still calls the number types "the tower", though they do not nest.
90	
91	**The team's `Int`, `Long`, `Float`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong` do not exist.** No library declares them. On both paths, each is undefined as a type: 'Float is undefined.' In their place, write `ZZ32` for `Int`, `ZZ64` for `Long`, `RR64` for `Float`, `ZZ` for `BigNum` and `NN64` for `UnsignedLong`. A `typecase` arm at such a name, or at any name that names no type in scope, gets the same message. Write an arm over every value as `x: Any =>`: the team's `x =>` reads `x` as a type, and is refused. In a tuple arm, an undefined name is still read as a binder that takes any element, on both paths, and no message names it undefined (row 1064). So under walk `(NoSuchType, ZZ32) =>` takes `("s", 3)`. Compiled, with an `Any` selector, the checker refuses that arm: 'The typecase clause, Pattern at ..., is unreachable.'
92	
93	**A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]`, or `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` with a radix point (P-174). Its static arguments are the numeral's numbers: `n` the digit count, `m` the count of digits after the point, `r` the radix, and `v` the digits read as one integer in that radix, so `3.125` is a `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. The compiler's prelude follows the same design (P-37).
94	
95	A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an infinity, overflow run-time arithmetic: for `t: RR64 = 10.0^308`, `t TIMES 10.0` is `Infinity` under walk. `x.isInfinite` tests for one. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`.
96	
97	Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value, other than a numeral type's number, is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).
98	
99	Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over its numbers, which its body declares, as `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v.asZZ32)`. With a radix point, write `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\])`. The coercion's body reads `n`, `r` and `v` as `ZZ` values without a bound, since a numeral's digits fit no fixed width (P-173, P-40). The `where` clause bounds the numerals that the type takes. The checker refuses statically a numeral that breaks it, as `300` here: 'The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte.' Walk refuses it when the binding runs. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches the type as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it (P-176). Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.
100	
101	**An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons, and `DIV`, `REM`, `MOD`, `GCD`, `LCM`, `CHOOSE` and `MINMAX` over integers. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. A quotient that is not whole stays `n / d` in lowest terms and defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. Except for a negated numeral, as `-3` above, a program's own type takes the constant only through a coercion from its default type, since coercions do not chain (P-174). So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
102	
103	**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). The rule converts at a declared return type too, but walk does not (row 387). Nor does walk convert a function argument from its arrow type to the parameter's, as `inc: ZZ32 -> ZZ32` passed at `f: ZZ32 -> ZZ64`: 'Unification error' (row 1083). Declare the function at the parameter's arrow type. Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". If one of them takes the call's numerals at their default, it runs instead: `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` is `RR64`'s product, not `QQ`'s.
104	
105	**A numeral can run a more specific declaration than the one that fits its default type (P-46).** On both paths, a call with a numeral runs the declaration that fits the numeral's default type, unless the numeral's coercion reaches another declaration whose declared parameter types are strict subtypes of the first one's. Then the other runs. So `k(5)` runs `k(x: NN32)` beside `k(x: Any)`, but `f(1.5)` runs `f(x: RR64)` beside `f(x: RR32)`. Two departures:
106	
107	- under walk, a numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, as `a = 0` for `a: Any` (row 1016);
108	- on both paths, `g(5)` runs `g[\T\](x: T)` beside `g(x: NN32)`, where the rule gives `g(x: NN32)` (row 1017).
109	
110	**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
111	
112	**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types declares its own functional method `asFloat(self): RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. A numeral reaches a number type's own `=` by its coercion (P-46). So on both paths `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u: NN32`. Under walk, `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead.
113	
114	**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
115	
116	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
117	
118	## Reductions and comprehensions
119	
120	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
121	
122	**Where a reduction's bound names its parameter, as for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places.** The argument is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, and the body's type only where there is no expected type or it does not fit the reduction's bound. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` sums `ZZ32` elements in `RR64`, not in the body's type. A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types; if it is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1".
123	
124	At a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment, the checker reads the declared type, so the two paths sum in different types (row 1008): `meth(): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#4] huge(j)` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk only. Write the argument there in a program for both paths. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one. So as a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths. Write both arguments of `BIG MIN_MAX`, the element types of its pairs, as `BIG MIN_MAX[\ZZ32, ZZ32\][j <- 0#3] pr(j)`: the checker infers only a single static parameter (row 1007). Departures under walk:
125	
126	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
127	- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
128	- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
129	
130	**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
131	
132	## Implementation limits
133	
134	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). Besides a `Boolean`, walk takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition.
135	
136	**Write every parameter type.** The compiled checker refuses a parameter without a type, "Missing parameter type for", unless the exported api's declaration gives the type. Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.

1	# Fortress microgpt: concurrency and memory handover
2	
3	As of 2026-11-18 · Pavol Vaškovič
4	
5	## Purpose
6	
7	This is context for a Claude Code session working in the Fortress revival repo (github.com/palimondo/fortress). The goal is to make Karpathy's microgpt run fast in Fortress on a multi-core machine (Apple Silicon).
8	
9	The conclusion of the discussion: keep STM (`atomic`) off the hot path entirely. A GPT training step is dense numeric work with no shared symbolic state. The fitting design is write-once flat arrays in a per-step arena, disjoint-write parallel loops, and a monoid reduction of gradients across the batch.
10	
11	The discussion was conceptual. Nobody read the Fortress source during it. Every statement about what the Fortress implementation does is an assumption to check, listed under Open questions.
12	
13	## STM background
14	
15	STM gives atomicity and isolation for a block of code without locks. It never went mainstream; it works where mutation is already controlled.
16	
17	**Mechanism (optimistic design).** Each shared variable has a version. A transaction logs its reads (variable + version) and buffers its writes privately. At commit it locks the written variables, checks that no read version changed, then publishes or discards and retries. The alternative writes in place and keeps an undo log. It is the database technique of optimistic concurrency control, without durability.
18	
19	**Where it works**
20	
21	- Haskell: the type system bans I/O inside transactions. Idiomatic and used in production.
22	- Clojure: multiversion STM over explicit `ref` cells that hold immutable values. Only ref operations are instrumented, and writing a ref outside a transaction throws. Rarely used in practice; atoms (one cell, CAS retry) cover most code.
23	
24	**Why it failed elsewhere** (Microsoft STM.NET cancelled 2010, C++ TM never standardised, PyPy-STM abandoned, Intel TSX disabled)
25	
26	- I/O cannot roll back, and unrestricted languages cannot forbid it inside a transaction.
27	- Instrumenting every read and write costs 2–10× single-threaded.
28	- Weak vs. strong atomicity: code outside transactions touching the same data breaks isolation; fixing it means instrumenting all code.
29	- Privatisation: removing an object from a shared structure in a transaction, then using it unsynchronised, was unsafe under the fast implementations.
30	- Joe Duffy's conclusion: the root problem is unrestricted shared mutable state. Get isolation and immutability first; transactions then serve the small remainder.
31	
32	The selling point was composability (two atomic blocks nest into one; two lock-based components do not compose), not raw speed against hand-tuned locking.
33	
34	## Fortress specifics
35	
36	Fortress supports an immutable, reduction-based style in which `atomic` is rarely needed. All of this is from general knowledge of the language, not from the repo.
37	
38	**STM in Fortress.** The original interpreter implemented `atomic` on a Java STM library derived from DSTM2 (Sun's Scalable Synchronization group), with threads on Doug Lea's fork/join pool. It ran, but no published result shows a multicore gain from it. The bet was on hardware TM in Sun's Rock processor, cancelled in 2009.
39	
40	**Immutable by default**
41	
42	- `x = e` is an immutable binding; mutable needs `var` or `:=`.
43	- Object fields are immutable unless declared `var` or `settable`.
44	- `value object` gives immutable value types.
45	- Arrays are mutable.
46	
47	**Why `atomic` appears.** Fortress is implicitly parallel: `for` bodies, tuple elements and function arguments may run in parallel. A shared accumulator therefore needs it:
48	
49	```
50	for i <- 1:n do atomic sum += a[i] end
51	```
52	
53	**The intended replacement** is a reduction over a generator, which splits the range, reduces the pieces in parallel and combines them with no shared variable:
54	
55	```
56	sum = SUM[i <- 1:n] a[i]
57	```
58	
59	**Other escapes**
60	
61	- `seq(1:n)` forces a sequential loop, where a local `var` accumulator is safe.
62	- Disjoint array writes (each iteration writes its own `a[i]`) need no `atomic`.
63	
64	**Strong-atomicity caveat.** The spec makes `atomic` atomic with respect to all other threads. An implementation may therefore route every mutable variable access through the STM, not only accesses inside `atomic` blocks. If this one does, the cost follows `var`, and removing `atomic` blocks alone will not remove it.
65	
66	## Ideas considered and set aside
67	
68	These are sound techniques for shared symbolic state. microgpt has none, so none of them is on the path.
69	
70	| Idea | What it is | Why not here |
71	| --- | --- | --- |
72	| Persistent collections (Clojure) | Immutable wide trees; an update copies one root-to-leaf path and shares the rest; one mutable root pointer updated by CAS | Pointer chasing and allocation; nobody does dense linear algebra on persistent vectors |
73	| Swift-style copy-on-write | In-place mutation when the buffer is uniquely referenced, full copy otherwise | Needs a reference count; the JVM has none. JVM substitutes: ownership tokens (Clojure transients), static uniqueness proof, compiler-inserted counting, or a sticky one-bit "shared" flag |
74	| Concurrent tries (Ctrie) | Per-node CAS with O(1) snapshots | For write-heavy shared maps, not tensors |
75	| Off-heap memory (Agrona, `Unsafe`) | Byte-oriented buffers outside the GC heap | `double[]`/`float[]` are already flat and unscanned by the GC, and HotSpot optimises them better than `Unsafe` access |
76	| LMAX Disruptor | Preallocated ring buffer, single writer, cache-line padding | A messaging structure; only its discipline transfers |
77	
78	**What does transfer** from the Disruptor school: allocate once, keep data flat, one writer per region, no garbage on the hot path.
79	
80	**Copy-on-write is unnecessary** because ownership is statically obvious in a training step. Activations are write-once. Only parameters and optimizer state outlive the step, and after the update nobody needs the old values, so they are updated in place.
81	
82	## Design direction for microgpt
83	
84	Treat the training step as a pure function over write-once flat arrays, and parallelise across training examples.
85	
86	**Memory**
87	
88	- Replace the scalar autograd graph (one heap object per scalar, linked by pointers) with a tape in flat parallel arrays: values, gradients, opcodes, operand indices.
89	- Allocate the tape once. Reset it each step by resetting an index. This is arena allocation.
90	- Parameters and optimizer state live in one uniquely owned block, updated in place between steps.
91	
92	**Parallelism**
93	
94	- Split loops so each task writes its own slice. Disjoint writes need no `atomic`.
95	- The hazard is the backward pass, where several consumers add into the same gradient cell. At scalar granularity that is a shared accumulator. At tensor granularity (matmul backward as one operation) it is disjoint-write loops again.
96	- The matrices are tiny, so threading inside one multiply will lose to scheduling overhead.
97	- Parallelism pays across examples: map over the batch, reduce per-example gradients with vector addition as the monoid. This is the generator/reducer pattern. The original is believed to train on one document per step, so this adds batching, a benign change to the algorithm.
98	
99	**GEMM**
100	
101	- Across cores, each output row or row block is independent, so associativity is not involved.
102	- Inside a core, the inner dot product is a reduction; strict IEEE ordering blocks SIMD. Declaring `+` associative licenses multiple accumulators and vector lanes.
103	- Loop order i-k-j makes the inner loop `C[i,:] += A[i,k] * B[k,:]`, which is elementwise and vectorises under strict IEEE.
104	
105	**Numerics**
106	
107	- Relaxed reduction order is normal in LLM training: GPU kernels reduce nondeterministically and runs are not bit-reproducible.
108	- Relax associativity only. Do not assume away NaN and infinity; that hides divergence.
109	- Keep long accumulations (loss sums, gradient sums over many examples) in higher precision.
110	- Prefer `float` over `double` where possible: on 128-bit NEON it doubles the lane count.
111	
112	## JVM tooling status
113	
114	On JDK 25, primitive arrays plus the incubating Vector API are what is available; value classes are not.
115	
116	| Tool | Status | Note |
117	| --- | --- | --- |
118	| Primitive arrays (`double[]`, `float[]`) | Stable | Flat, unboxed, not scanned by the GC. The default choice |
119	| Vector API (`jdk.incubator.vector`) | Tenth incubator in JDK 25 ([JEP 508](https://openjdk.org/jeps/508)) | Needs `--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector` at compile and run time. Package will be renamed on leaving incubation |
120	| Foreign Function & Memory API (`MemorySegment`, `Arena`) | Final | Supported replacement for `Unsafe` memory access. Worth it only to hand memory to native BLAS |
121	| Value classes ([Project Valhalla](https://openjdk.org/projects/valhalla/), JEP 401) | Preview in JDK 28, due March 2027; early-access builds exist | Not in JDK 25. Needs `--enable-preview`. Expected to stay in preview through JDK 29 |
122	
123	**Vector API discipline.** A vector is an ordinary heap object today. Speed depends on the C2 compiler proving it never escapes. Keep vectors as local variables inside the hot loop, load from and store to primitive arrays, and never put a vector in a field or collection. Otherwise each operation allocates.
124	
125	**Why the Vector API waits for Valhalla.** Value classes let the VM keep vectors in registers as a property of the type instead of an optimisation that may fail. Finalising the API before that would freeze a shape that then has to break.
126	
127	**Where Valhalla would matter here.** Only if a Fortress value object (a dual number for autograd, say) should live flat inside an array.
128	
129	Not verified: the JEP 401 page returned a stale copy when fetched, so the Valhalla status rests on the project page and August 2026 press coverage.

1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.
5	
6	**distance stage**
7	: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.
8	
9	The code of this area is in these directories:
10	
11	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
12	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
13	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
14	
15	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
16	
17	## What the two paths share
18	
19	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
20	
21	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`), which the classes of the prelude's number objects extend.
22	- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`ZZ32.java`, `ZZ64.java`).
23	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
24	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
25	
26	Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.
27	
28	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
29	
30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it uses the one library in their place. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
33	
34	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and its seven number types are each one `value object`, as in the interpreter's library. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.
35	
36	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37	
38	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39	
40	- `spawn`;
41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`;
43	- a built-in number type named as a value, as `x: Object = ZZ32`: 'Can't compile the number type ZZ32 as a value yet' (ledger row 1082).
44	
45	Against the compiler's prelude, it refuses a varargs parameter: 'Can't compile VarArgs yet: the library in use, CompilerLibrary, declares no ImmutableArray, ...'. With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, it compiles a varargs parameter, though such a program does not run yet (`SKILL.md`, "How a program runs"). There it stops with `OptionUnwrapException` on a varargs method, or a generic varargs function, where another declaration of its name has the same number of parameters, the varargs parameter counted as one (ledger row 1086). Give the varargs declaration its own name.
46	
47	It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
48	
49	- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
50	- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
51	- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
52	
53	A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):
54	
55	- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
56	- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
57	- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet';
58	- a call, at an assumption of a generic trait, of a method whose parameter has the trait's type parameter, as `stamp(Q asif Tagged[\String\], s asif String)` for `stamp(self, x: T)` in `Tagged[\T\]`: 'Can't find the body that Tagged[\String\] gives stamp at ...' (ledger row 1088).
59	
60	At an assumption of a trait, the call runs the trait's body, also where the object overrides it.
61	
62	It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
63	
64	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
65	
66	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
67	
68	## What the code generator does
69	
70	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
71	- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of a coercion that raises sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
72	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
73	- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
74	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
75	
76	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
77	
78	## The runtime
79	
80	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes, for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417), and to choose a call's opcode from the class file of the called method's class, without loading that class. Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
81	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`), and an object's `var` field in a cell that the object holds. Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.
82	
83	## Natives
84	
85	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
86	
87	A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
88	
89	- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
90	- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
91	- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
92	- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).
93	
94	The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.
95	
96	To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.
97	
98	The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:
99	
100	- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
101	- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
102	- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
103	- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
104	
105	The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these three types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
106	
107	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

109	## Traps of the compiled path
110	
111	- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
112	- Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `=/=` at `RR32` and `RR64`, so the checker refuses `r =/= 0` for an `RR64` value `r` (ledger row 1059). Write `NOT (r = 0)`. At `RR32`, `=` compiles and overflows the stack when it runs (ledger row 528). Bind an `RR32` value `c` at `RR64` first, as `r: RR64 = c`, and compare `r`.
113	- A parameter of a declared tuple type is one JVM parameter for each element (F-378). So in a `VerifyError`, the method's descriptor lists each element of a tuple parameter as a parameter of its own. These three tuple forms fail:
114	  - an object's method overloaded at a pair and at another type fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1054). Give the two methods two names;
115	  - an object whose one value parameter is a pair dies in its constructor with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 1055). Add a second value parameter beside the pair, as `object Holder(n: ZZ32, var pr: (ZZ32, ZZ32))`;
116	  - a generic operator whose one parameter has its type parameter's type, applied to a pair, dies at the call with `NoSuchMethodError`, as `pr!!` for `opr (x: T)!![\T\] : T = x` and `pr = (1, 2)` (ledger row 1056). Write no such call in a compiled program.
117	- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when one of these leaves the `try` block: an `exit`, an exception that no `catch` clause takes, or the `ForbiddenException` that the `try` throws (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception or an `exit` leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
118	- To fork is to run as tasks that can run at once. A call's arguments and an operator's operands fork, as the rule says, where two or more of them are calls, written `f(x)`, of functions that the program declares. So write no compiled program that relies on the order in which its arguments are evaluated. Until the switch-over, the calls written in the compiler's prelude do not fork, so a compiled `SUM` runs one body at a time (ledger row 982). A compiled parallel `for` runs its bodies at once: use it in a test of parallelism.
119	- An `atomic` block (`atomic do ... end`) or atomic expression (`atomic e`, as `atomic 1`), a `try` or a `label` block as a call's argument after the first, as `f(k, atomic do ... end)`, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load, unless the arguments fork (ledger row 322). So does a `try` as an operator's operand after the first (ledger row 526). Bind its value in a statement of its own.

121	  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.

It also refuses a tuple binding to a `case` or a `try` whose branches are numeral tuples, as `(a, b) = case k of 1 => (1, 2) else => (3, 4) end`: 'Right-hand side has type OR(...), but left-hand side is a tuple of 2 variables.' The checker refuses a call on `x'` of a method of `X`'s bound, as `x'.name()` for a method `name` of `Shape` (ledger row 1072). Call it on the selector, as `x.name()`.
137	- In a trait with a `comprises` clause, the checker refuses a getter of a listed type read on `self`: `self.d` in `trait Q comprises { R }`, `d` a field of `R`, gives '(Q & {R}) has no getter called d' (ledger row 1071). Bind `self` at the listed type first, as `r: R = self`, and read `r.d`.
138	- A function expression whose type is an intersection dies when its closure is made. Such a type comes from a call typed by the intersection of its candidates' return types, as `fn () => choose(m)`, where `choose` has declarations at two traits that `m`'s type extends, each with its own return type (`compiler_tests/XXXIntersectionClosureResult.fss`): 'Unable to read serialized data for Intersection??' (ledger row 559). Write none in a compiled program.
139	- Until the switch-over, the prelude's `String` gives `<`, `=`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` and `=/=` the placeholder body `false`. A string value is a `JavaString`, whose own declarations compare. A call at an assumption runs the trait's body ("What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), so `("ab" asif String) < ("cd" asif String)` is `false` (ledger row 1089). Compare strings without an assumption.
140	- A tuple expression as the argument of a parameter of type `Any` stops the code generator: 'Error trying to close method scope' (ledger row 1080). Bind it first, as `p: Any = (k, k)`, and pass `p`.
141	- Where a function of no parameters is passed at a parameter of an arrow type that its own type coerces to, as a `() -> ZZ32` at `() -> ZZ64`, the program dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` when the callee calls it (ledger row 1084). At one parameter, the coercion runs. Declare the function at the parameter's arrow type.
142	- A spread argument to a varargs parameter, as `f(1, ys...)`, passes none of the elements of `ys`: walk drops it, and so does the checker with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` (ledger row 1085). Pass the elements as arguments.

145	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
146	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. These die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
147	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);

A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839);
